lead: A compiler cannot give a name an address until it knows which run of a procedure that name belongs to. Source languages supply procedures, parameters, scope rules and binding rules; the compiler turns them into a tree of activations and a stack of live records. This chapter settles the questions the compiler must answer before it generates code: what an activation is, how activations form a tree, which records stay live on the control stack, and how scope differs from lifetime. The answers fix the shape of every runtime environment in the rest of this unit.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 (the phases of a compiler) and Unit 4 (translating procedure calls into three-address code); 5.2 then places these records in memory.

blocks.text: A procedure is a named piece of code that takes parameters and does work on behalf of its caller; it may or may not return a result. Functions in C, methods in Java and subroutines in Fortran are all procedures. The procedure is the unit of abstraction: the caller says what it wants done and the body hides how.

A definition supplies the body and asks the compiler to produce code. A declaration only announces the name, the parameter types and the result type, so that calls elsewhere can be checked. In C, int fare(int); is a declaration; int fare(int n) { return 30 * n; } is a definition. A program may declare a procedure many times and define it once.

An activation is one execution of a procedure, from entry to return. Each activation keeps its own copies of the parameters and the locals. Recursion shows why: when a procedure calls itself, the second activation gets a fresh copy of every local, so it cannot overwrite the first one's. The first activation is suspended, not finished, and its values must survive intact until it resumes.

sections.h3: The activation tree and the control stack

blocks.text: Put one node for the activation of the main program. When an activation calls a procedure, add a child node for the new activation; siblings sit left to right in call order. The result is the activation tree, and its preorder traversal lists the activations in the order in which they begin.

At any instant, the activations that have begun and not yet returned lie on a single path from the root to the activation that is running. They are held in the control stack: a record is pushed on entry and popped on return, so the stack always holds exactly that path. The depth of the activation tree — the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path — is the largest number of records alive at once, and it sizes the stack. 5.4 shows what each record contains.

The call graph has one node per procedure and an edge wherever one procedure can call another. The activation tree has one node per activation, so a recursive procedure appears in it as many times as it is called.

With lexical scope, also called static scope, a use of a name is resolved from the program text: look in the enclosing block, then in the block around that, and so on outward. The position is fixed by the text alone. 5.6 covers the symbol table that implements this.

The environment is the map from a name to a storage location; the state is the value currently at that location. Under lexical scope the distance from a use to its declaration never changes. The compiler stores that distance as a pair (nesting depth, offset) and emits code that starts from the running activation's record and follows that many access links to reach the frame holding the declaration. The distance is static; the address is computed at run time with no search of the stack.

Lifetime is the time between allocation and release of storage. Scope is the part of the text where a declaration is visible. They are independent. A C function that returns the address of its local ends the lifetime of that storage when its record is popped, while the pointer in the caller is still in scope and now dangles. In the other direction, an inner block's storage may still exist after its name has gone out of scope. Text controls the name; the run controls the storage.

Two names denote one location: a pointer and its target, a reference parameter, a union in C. A write through one name changes what the other sees, so the compiler cannot trust a copy held in a register across a call.

sections.h3: Dynamic scoping, procedure parameters and closures

blocks.text: Dynamic scoping resolves a name through the chain of callers at run time, not through the text. The same name then refers to different declarations on different calls, so its depth is unknown at compile time and every non-local access becomes a run-time search. A few older languages and some shell languages work this way; it makes fast access and static type checking harder, which is why lexical scope dominates.

A procedure may be passed to another procedure and called through the parameter. To make that call, the callee needs the code address and, under lexical scope, the environment where the procedure was defined. That pair is a closure. Only a few universities teach closures in the compiler course.

figure.caption: The activation tree for the call main(): six activations, children in call order, and the path main → a(1) → b → c giving the deepest stack of four records.

spec.aria: An activation tree: main calls a(1) and then c; a(1) calls b and then a(0); b calls c, giving six activations in all.

examples.question: A program has procedures main, a, b and c. main calls a(1) and then c. a(x) calls b() and then a(x − 1) when x > 0. b() calls c(). c() does nothing. Draw the activation tree for the call main(), give the order in which the activations begin, and give the largest number of records on the control stack.
steps: main begins: activation 1, depth 1, the root of the tree.
main calls a(1): activation 2, a child of main, depth 2.
Inside a(1), x = 1 > 0, so it calls b(): activation 3, a child of a(1), depth 3.
b() calls c(): activation 4, a child of b, depth 4. c returns at once.
b returns. a(1) now calls a(0): activation 5, a second child of a(1), depth 3.
In a(0), x = 0, so the condition fails and the body makes no calls. It returns.
a(1) returns. main calls c: activation 6, a child of main, depth 2. It returns.
Preorder of the tree gives the order of beginning: main, a(1), b, c, a(0), c — six activations.
The longest root-to-leaf path is main → a(1) → b → c, which has 4 nodes, so at most 4 records are live at once.
examples.answer: Six activations begin in the order main, a(1), b, c, a(0), c, and the control stack holds at most 4 records.
examples.check:
calls = []
depth = 0
maxdepth = 0

def enter(name):
    global depth, maxdepth
    depth += 1
    if depth > maxdepth:
        maxdepth = depth
    calls.append(name)

def leave():
    global depth
    depth -= 1

def c():
    enter("c"); leave()

def b():
    enter("b"); c(); leave()

def a(x):
    enter("a(%d)" % x)
    if x > 0:
        b()
        a(x - 1)
    leave()

def main():
    enter("main"); a(1); c(); leave()

main()
print(len(calls))
print(maxdepth)

traps: Drawing the call graph and calling it the activation tree. The call graph has one node per procedure; the activation tree has one node per activation, so a recursive procedure appears many times.

Saying a name is in scope, therefore its storage exists. Scope is text, lifetime is the run. A name is in scope in a block not yet entered, while its storage does not exist yet; and storage can linger while a pointer to it is in scope after the name itself has gone out of scope. A local's name is not in scope in the caller after the call returns.
Counting the depth of the activation tree in edges instead of nodes. The number of live records equals the number of nodes on the path, not the number of edges.
Treating a declaration as a definition. A declaration only fixes the type; code and storage appear only at the definition.
Assuming dynamic scoping can be resolved at compile time. The declaration a use binds to depends on the caller chain, so the depth is unknown until the call happens.

quiz.q: Define an activation and an activation tree.
quiz.a: An activation is one execution of a procedure, from entry to return, with its own copies of parameters and locals. The activation tree has one node per activation, with children in call order.

quiz.q: Give one difference between a declaration and a definition of a procedure.
quiz.a: A declaration gives only the name, parameter types and result type; a definition gives the body and causes code to be generated. A procedure may be declared many times and defined once.

quiz.q: Why must each activation of a recursive procedure have its own copy of the locals?
quiz.a: The outer activation is suspended, not finished, and must find its values unchanged when it resumes. A shared copy would be overwritten by the inner call.

quiz.q: main calls p(2). p(n) calls q() and then p(n − 1) when n > 0. q() calls r(). Give the activation order and the maximum number of live records.
quiz.a: Activations: main, p(2), q, r, p(1), q, r, p(0) — 8 in all. The longest path is main → p(2) → q → r, so 4 records.

quiz.q: In the worked example, how many records are on the control stack while activation 5, a(0), is running?
quiz.a: Three records: main, a(1) and a(0), the path from the root to the running activation.

quiz.q: A C function returns the address of its local variable. Use scope and lifetime to explain why dereferencing that pointer is undefined.
quiz.a: The lifetime of the local's storage ends when the call returns and the record is popped. The caller's pointer is in scope but now points at storage that no longer belongs to that variable and may be reused by the next call, so dereferencing it is undefined.

quiz.q: Why can the compiler not fix a (depth, offset) pair for a non-local name under dynamic scoping?
quiz.a: The declaration a use binds to depends on the caller chain at run time. Different calls reach different declarations at different depths, so the binding must be searched on the stack at run time.

quiz.q: Why does a recursive procedure appear many times in the activation tree but once in the call graph?
quiz.a: The call graph is per procedure, one node each. The activation tree is per activation, and every call creates a new activation.

beyond: Not for the exam. Compilers for functional languages turn each closure into a heap record holding a code pointer and the free variables, a step called closure conversion or lambda lifting. The JVM, Go and V8 do not keep every record on the stack: escape analysis moves a frame to the heap when a pointer to it can outlive the call. Shadow stacks and return-address protection reuse the same stack discipline. Search for escape analysis, closure conversion and display registers to go further.
